cards.back: The region of the program where the variable is valid — where it can be read or written
cards.extra: Outside that region the name does not resolve; the compiler rejects the reference rather than failing at runtime.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::07 Variables and Scopes

cards.front: What scope does a variable declared in the class body, outside any method, have?
cards.back: Class scope — usable anywhere in the class, and visible beyond it depending on the access modifier
cards.extra: private keeps it inside the class; no modifier makes it package-visible. It is one instance per object unless static.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::07 Variables and Scopes

cards.front: What scope does a variable declared inside a method have?
cards.back: Method scope — valid only inside that method's body
cards.extra: Another method cannot see it at all, even if the name is the same. This is the most common scope you work with.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::07 Variables and Scopes

cards.front: What is a loop variable's scope?
cards.back: Only the loop body and header — it does not exist after the loop
cards.extra: Declared in a for-each or in the for initialiser, it is gone at the closing brace. Referring to it afterwards is a compile error.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::07 Variables and Scopes

cards.front: Does a bare { } block create a new scope?
cards.back: Yes — any pair of braces is a scope
cards.extra: Variables declared inside are invisible outside, and the block can reuse names that exist outside it. This is how you limit a temporary's lifetime.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::07 Variables and Scopes

cards.back: A variable in an inner scope reusing the name of one in an outer scope, hiding it
cards.extra: Inside the inner block the outer variable can no longer be named directly. It is legal and usually a mistake.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::07 Variables and Scopes

cards.front: How do you reach a field that a local variable has shadowed?
cards.extra: The field is still there; only the unqualified name resolves to the local. The this prefix is also the idiomatic fix inside setters and constructors.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::07 Variables and Scopes

cards.front: Why is shadowing considered bad practice?
cards.back: The same name means different things in adjacent lines, so a reader cannot tell which variable a statement touches
cards.extra: Prefer distinct names. Where a parameter must match the field name, this.field = field; makes the intent explicit.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::07 Variables and Scopes
